headline: Leading mathematicians are split over OpenAI's claim that its AI has solved one of mathematics' seven Millennium Prize Problems.
score_reason: Lowered from 7: OpenAI's claim dates from 8 Sep 2026 and is still unverified, so today's news is the mathematicians' reaction, reported from a mid-September forum.
importance_line: Working mathematicians, especially early in their careers, describe pressure to use paid AI tools and the risk of being beaten to results, and one leading mathematician says how people are assessed, hired and taught must be rethought, but OpenAI's claim is unverified and the company did not comment.
summary: IEEE Spectrum reports that mathematicians at Germany's Heidelberg Laureate Forum are split over OpenAI's claim, reported by the BBC on 8 Sep 2026, that about 10,000 of its AI agents solved the Navier-Stokes problem (a long-open question about fluid flow and one of seven famously hard Millennium Prize Problems) in 88 hours, which it says would be a watershed if verified. Peter Scholze, a winner of the Fields Medal (a top mathematics prize), called such announcements 'some kind of PR stunt', Geordie Williamson said OpenAI 'behaved extremely poorly', and Jacob Tsimerman said that, without knowing the details, solving it 'feels pretty definitive'; OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment.
notes: Read in full. Feature on the reaction to OpenAI's 8 Sep 2026 claim (the forum began 13 Sep); the article itself gives no date and no 88 hours, which are from the BBC report of 8 Sep (read). Same claim as the 5 Oct pool item 'OpenAI says AI agents solved centuries-old mathematical problem in 88 hours' (ANA, 4 Oct); no edition since 23 Sep carried it. BBC also reported that OpenAI said it had not seen Buckmaster and Alpöge's work before they released it; IEEE Spectrum quotes only the critics on that point and says OpenAI did not respond. Score lowered by one for the stale claim, the unverified result and an IEEE headline that states the solution as fact.
